title: Why Games Praise the Player | Designing Success Feedback

scenes.title: Score and Recognition Are Distinct
lines: Nintendo Switch Sports shows a win banner and a celebration after a match.
Ring Fit Adventure accompanies exercise movements with evaluation feedback.
The same score can feel different when a game acknowledges what you did.
We can distinguish calculating success from expressing recognition of that success.
Today we examine how to recognize an action, rather than how to add rewards.
Our original defense test applies the same inputs and collision rules to both screens.
We change the timing, wording, strength, and position of the praise.
Enjoyment needs human testing, while logs can verify exactly what changed.

scenes.title: Respond Close to the Success
lines: First, compare when the praise appears.
Both characters block the same attack at the same moment.
One side responds promptly; the other responds much later.
If the next attack arrives during the wait, it is harder to connect praise with the action.
Try attaching a brief response close to the successful collision result.
The signal can acknowledge the recent action without a large display.
This does not prescribe one delay for every game.
It is a reason to check overlap with the next action at normal speed.

scenes.title: Name the Action That Succeeded
lines: A generic compliment may not explain what went well.
This test blocks an attack, then moves upward to dodge the next one.
One screen repeats the same praise; the other distinguishes blocking from dodging.
A brief label names the action actually verified by the collision rules.
Calling a button press a perfect block can misrepresent the result.
Choose the label from the successful outcome, rather than the input event alone.
That information can help the player identify an action to try again.
Praise need not become an instruction manual, but it need not hide its reason.

scenes.title: Match Strength to Accomplishment
lines: Using the largest celebration for every success removes a distinction between moments.
A match win in Switch Sports illustrates a broader celebration at a stopping point.
The same scale after every small success can cover the next situation.
Our test uses a small marker for a single block.
A stronger response appears only when a sequence of successful blocks is verified.
The score and successful-action count stay equal; only presentation strength changes.
Distinguish an individual success, a sequence, and the completion of a longer section.
This aligns the scale of the recognition with the actual accomplishment.

scenes.title: Be Supportive Without Hiding Failure
lines: Unconditionally calling a failure perfect can undermine trust in the praise.
Both screens receive the same inputs, deliberately missing one attack.
Health falls equally, but one side still claims the performance was perfect.
The other side shows the hit and acknowledges only the blocks that actually succeeded.
We can name a genuine partial success without hiding the failure.
Every failure does not need a compliment.
Show a retry clue separately, and distinguish signals for success and failure.
Supportive wording should remain connected to actual outcomes to inform another attempt.

scenes.title: Leave Room for the Next Action
lines: Finally, check whether the praise obstructs the next action.
Large text placed over the attack can cover the area where the next threat must be read.
This comparison preserves outcomes and wording while changing position and area.
Compare a small marker near the action with a brief response near the edge.
Check that neither moving targets nor necessary information are obscured at phone size.
Record what is recognized, when it is recognized, and how strongly it is expressed.
Before increasing praise frequency, check whether the expression matches the recent action.
Look for moments of accomplishment in the actual actions of your own game.
